learn: World literature lets readers enter perspectives shaped by different histories, languages and values.
Reading across cultures builds empathy and challenges assumptions about what is "normal".
Translations are interpretations; translators make choices about word, rhythm and tone.
lessons.try: Compare two translations of the same short passage and note the differences.

learn: Context includes the historical, social, political and religious setting of a work and its author.
Understanding context helps explain characters' values and conflicts.
Avoid judging a text only by your own culture's standards; first seek to understand.
check: Context includes the ___ setting of a work.
Before judging a text, first seek to...
lessons.try: Research the context of a story before reading it, then note how context changes your reading.

learn: Great works are both particular (rooted in a time and place) and universal (speaking across cultures).
Rabindranath Tagore's stories, such as "The Postmaster" (1891), portray Bengali village life and universal loneliness.
Analyse how specific cultural details carry universal themes.
check: Particular details are rooted in a...
lessons.try: Read "The Postmaster" and identify universal and particular elements.

units.t: Ancient Epics: Gilgamesh and the Hero

learn: The "Epic of Gilgamesh" from ancient Mesopotamia is one of the oldest surviving works of literature, recorded on clay tablets.
Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, befriends the wild man Enkidu; after Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh searches for immortality.
The epic explores friendship, mortality and what makes a life meaningful.
lessons.try: Summarise Gilgamesh's quest and what he learns.

learn: Joseph Campbell described a common pattern: the call to adventure, trials, a crisis, transformation and return.
Many myths and modern stories follow this pattern.
The pattern helps compare heroes across cultures.
check: The hero's journey begins with the...
The hero is usually ___ by the journey.
The pattern helps compare heroes across...
lessons.try: Map a film or novel onto the hero's journey.

learn: Conventions include a hero of great stature, a vast setting, supernatural forces, long journeys and elevated style.
The flood story in Gilgamesh parallels other ancient flood narratives.
Compare Gilgamesh with Odysseus or Beowulf.
check: Gilgamesh includes a story of a...
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing two epic heroes.

learn: Greek tragedy developed in Athens in the 400s BCE, performed at festivals for Dionysus.
Plays alternated episodes of dialogue with choral odes; the chorus comments on the action.
Aristotle's "Poetics" described tragedy as arousing pity and fear leading to catharsis.
lessons.try: Explain the role of the chorus in one scene.

learn: Sophocles's "Oedipus Rex" (about 429 BCE) follows a king who seeks the truth about a plague and discovers he has fulfilled a terrible prophecy.
Dramatic irony is intense: the audience knows the truth long before Oedipus does.
Themes include fate, free will, knowledge and blindness.
lessons.try: Trace images of sight and blindness through the play.

learn: A tragic hero is admirable but has a flaw (hamartia) that leads to downfall.
Hubris (excessive pride) is a common flaw.
Anagnorisis is the moment of recognition; peripeteia is the reversal of fortune.
lessons.try: Apply Aristotle's terms to Oedipus.

learn: A strong literary thesis makes an arguable claim about how and why a text creates meaning.
Formula: Through [technique], [author] [verb] [insight].
Avoid obvious claims; aim for interpretation.
check: A thesis explains how and ___ a text creates meaning.
lessons.try: Write three thesis statements and rank them by strength.

learn: Choose evidence that best supports the claim; embed it smoothly.
Commentary explains how evidence supports the claim, analysing word choice and technique.
Aim for more commentary than quotation.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph with two embedded quotes and full commentary.

learn: Introduction with context and thesis; body paragraphs each with a claim; conclusion that extends the argument.
Transitions link ideas logically.
The conclusion answers "so what?"
lessons.try: Outline an analytical essay on a text from this course.

units.t: Shakespeare’s World: Julius Caesar or Macbeth

learn: Shakespeare wrote tragedies including "Julius Caesar" (1599) and "Macbeth" (about 1606).
Both explore ambition, power and the consequences of violence.
Elizabethan and Jacobean audiences valued order and feared rebellion.
lessons.try: Research the Globe Theatre and how plays were staged.

learn: The witches' prophecy sparks Macbeth's ambition; Lady Macbeth pushes him to murder King Duncan.
Guilt appears through hallucinations: the dagger, Banquo's ghost, and Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking.
Imagery of blood and darkness runs throughout.
check: Lady Macbeth's guilt shows in her...
lessons.try: Trace blood imagery in three scenes.

learn: Brutus joins the conspiracy to kill Caesar, believing it serves Rome.
After the assassination, Brutus and Mark Antony give funeral speeches; Antony's "Friends, Romans, countrymen" uses irony to turn the crowd.
The play questions whether noble motives justify violence.
lessons.try: Compare the rhetoric of Brutus's and Antony's speeches.

learn: Every argument has a speaker, audience, purpose, context and exigence (the urgent issue prompting it).
Analyse how the situation shapes choices.
Sojourner Truth's speech at the 1851 Women's Convention in Ohio addressed race and gender together.
lessons.try: Analyse the rhetorical situation of a historic speech.

learn: Appeals: ethos, pathos, logos, and kairos (timeliness).
Devices: anaphora, antithesis, rhetorical questions, parallelism, concession.
Analyse not just what devices appear, but why they work for the audience.
lessons.try: Write a rhetorical analysis paragraph on one speech.

learn: State a precise claim, support it with evidence and reasoning, and address counterclaims.
Use a mix of evidence: data, expert testimony, examples, analogies.
Maintain an appropriate tone for the audience.
lessons.try: Write an argument on a contemporary issue for a school newspaper.

units.t: Things Fall Apart and Postcolonial Literature

learn: Chinua Achebe's "Things Fall Apart" (1958) depicts Igbo society in Nigeria before and during British colonisation.
Achebe wrote partly to counter European portrayals of Africa as without culture or history.
The title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming" (1919).
check: The novel is set among the...
The title comes from a poem by...
lessons.try: Research Igbo society in the late 1800s.

learn: Okonkwo is a respected warrior driven by fear of appearing weak like his father.
His rigidity and violence lead to exile and, finally, tragedy when he cannot adapt to change.
Readers debate whether he is a tragic hero in the classical sense.
check: Okonkwo's flaw is often seen as...
The novel shows a culture facing...
lessons.try: Argue whether Okonkwo is a tragic hero, with evidence.

learn: Postcolonial literature examines the effects of colonialism on cultures and identities.
Themes include cultural conflict, language, power and resistance.
Writers often reclaim their history from colonial narratives.
lessons.try: Compare how two texts portray cultural collision.

learn: Poems from Persia, China, Japan, India and elsewhere offer different forms and traditions.
Rumi (1207-1273) wrote mystical poetry in Persian; Li Bai (701-762) wrote Chinese poems about nature and wine.
Translations capture meaning but may lose sound and form.
lessons.try: Read poems by Rumi and Li Bai and compare their imagery.

learn: The ghazal (Arabic, Persian, Urdu) uses couplets with a repeated refrain.
Japanese haiku and tanka capture moments in nature.
The sonnet spread from Italy across Europe.
lessons.try: Write a ghazal or a tanka.

learn: Analyse speaker, situation, imagery, sound, structure and shifts.
Consider cultural context and translation.
Write an interpretation supported by close reading.
check: A shift is a change in...
lessons.try: Write an analysis of a poem in translation.

units.t: Modern World Novels and Narrative Technique

learn: Novelists choose narrators carefully: first person, third person limited, omniscient, multiple narrators.
Stream of consciousness follows a character's flowing thoughts.
Franz Kafka's "The Metamorphosis" (1915) uses a detached voice to describe an absurd transformation.
check: Following a character's flowing thoughts is...
lessons.try: Read the opening of "The Metamorphosis" and analyse its narrative voice.

learn: Novels can be linear or nonlinear, using flashbacks, frame narratives or fragments.
A frame narrative tells a story within a story.
Structure shapes suspense and meaning.
check: A story within a story is a...
lessons.try: Diagram the structure of a novel you've read.

learn: Allegories use characters and events to represent abstract ideas or real situations.
Symbols deepen meaning across a novel.
Readers interpret symbols using textual evidence.
check: Kafka's transformation can be read as...
lessons.try: Explain an allegory in a novel or story.

learn: Develop a focused research question about literature, history or culture.
Use scholarly sources: peer-reviewed articles, academic books, reputable databases.
Evaluate sources for authority, accuracy, purpose and currency.
lessons.try: Find and evaluate five scholarly sources on your topic.

learn: Synthesis combines sources to support your own argument.
Use sources in conversation: agree, disagree, extend.
Your voice should lead; sources support.
check: In a research paper, ___ should lead.
lessons.try: Write a synthesis paragraph using three sources.

learn: MLA uses in-text citations (Author page) and a Works Cited page.
Format: double-spaced, 12-point font, header with name, teacher, course, date.
Revise for argument, organisation, evidence and style; then proofread.
lessons.try: Complete and format a 1,500-word research paper.
